analysis.one_liner: Stops medical debt from appearing on credit reports or being used for loan decisions.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 29, 2025 with 17 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal credit-reporting law so medical bills — including ones sent to a collection agency — can no longer show up on your credit report. It would also require the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, within one year, to bar lenders from looking at your medical debt when deciding whether to give you credit. It would not erase anyone's medical debt.
analysis.who_benefits: Households carrying medical bills in collection — often from emergencies, insurance denials, or disputed bills — would see that debt vanish from their credit reports. Credit scores typically rise when collections come off, which improves access to mortgages, car loans, credit cards, and rental housing. Roughly one in five American adults has medical debt in some form, and it is the most common type of debt on consumer credit reports.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households with medical bills in collection

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act so that no adverse medical-debt information — including a debt placed for collection or charged off — may appear on a consumer report.
It directs the CFPB to amend its regulations within one year of enactment so creditors are prohibited from obtaining or using a consumer's medical debt when deciding whether to extend credit.
The ban covers medical debt 'related to, in whole or in part' the receipt of medical services, products, or devices, so it reaches mixed bills and blended accounts, not just pure hospital charges.

analysis.who_pays: Credit reporting agencies would lose a stream of data they sell in reports; medical debt collectors would lose the credit-report threat, their main lever for pressuring people to pay; lenders would lose an underwriting input they have treated as predictive of repayment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus, debt collectors, and lenders

drawbacks.text: The bill does not forgive medical debt; people would still owe the money and collectors could still call and sue — the bill only removes the debt from credit reporting, so unpaid bills keep accruing elsewhere.

Barring lenders from using medical debt removes an underwriting signal some lenders consider predictive of repayment risk, and lenders could price that uncertainty into other borrowers' credit decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete for a large group: medical collections on credit reports depress scores even when the underlying bill is small or disputed, and removing them measurably improves access to housing and credit. The costs fall on industries rather than the public, though the strongest good-faith objection is that lenders genuinely lose information about borrowers who appear to ignore debts. The bill is narrow — it changes reporting and underwriting rules, not the debt itself — so it fixes a scoring problem, not the problem of people owing medical bills in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: It sits with the House Financial Services Committee, which has taken no action beyond receiving the referral.

narrative.text: Rep. Nikema Williams of Georgia introduced the bill on July 29, 2025.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services, and no further action appears in the record.
Seventeen Democrats joined as cosponsors; no Republicans are listed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has moved either way yet. As the bill sits without committee action, the status quo holds: credit bureaus and medical debt collectors keep their current data and collection tools, while borrowers with medical collections continue to carry the credit-score hit. If it never advances, those industries will have been spared a change by the absence of a vote rather than a decision on the merits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit bureaus and debt collectors, for now

for.name: Rep. Nikema Williams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 29, 2025 and recruited 17 cosponsors.

for.name: 17 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original and subsequent cosponsors, all Democrats.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee (Chair French Hill)
against.role: Committee of referral; chair has not scheduled a markup
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 29, 2025; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 names on the bill are Democrats; no Republican cosponsors appear, and the bill sits in a committee run by the other party with no action taken.

industries.industry: Credit bureaus and consumer reporting agencies
industries.note: Their credit report products currently include medical collections, which depress scores and drive consumer purchases of score services; the bill strips this data out entirely, removing the report entry and the distress it causes rather than a product people can pay to fix.

The threat of a credit report hit is the primary lever for getting people to pay old medical bills; without it, medical debt becomes much harder to collect, cutting directly into collections on a large volume of consumer accounts.
They would be barred from obtaining or using medical debt information in credit decisions, removing an underwriting input some lenders treat as predictive of repayment risk.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills referred to committee in a Congress never receive a vote, and this one has none of the ingredients that usually change that: no Republican cosponsors, no committee hearing, and a House majority unlikely to bring up a bill its members have not touched. Expect it to die at the end of this Congress unless its sponsor reintroduces it with broader backing next session.
